extraction.name: Visual Genome
extraction.description: A dataset for comprehensive scene understanding with densely annotated images, including objects, attributes, relationships, region descriptions, scene graphs, and question-answer pairs. It contains over 100K images with dense annotations to support cognitive tasks such as image description and question answering.
extraction.creator: Ranjay Krishna; Yuke Zhu; Oliver Groth; Justin Johnson; Kenji Hata; Joshua Kravitz; Stephanie Chen; Yannis Kalantidis; Li-Jia Li; David A. Shamma; Michael S. Bernstein; Li Fei-Fei
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was created and verified through a multi-stage crowdsourcing pipeline on Amazon Mechanical Turk, where workers annotated components such as region descriptions, objects, attributes, relationships, scene graphs, questions, and answers. Images were selected from the intersection of MS-COCO and YFCC.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The source data consisted of 108,249 real-world, non-iconic Flickr images taken from the intersection of the MS-COCO and YFCC image collections.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations were created through multiple Amazon Mechanical Turk task stages for each component. Workers wrote region descriptions and QA pairs, extracted objects from descriptions and grounded them with bounding boxes, added attributes and relationships based on description text, and all annotations then went through verification using majority voting and rapid judgments. Workers were given specific instructions such as bounding box coverage/quality requirements and QA writing rules.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Annotation quality was assessed through a verification stage applied to all data, using majority voting and rapid judgments to eliminate incorrect, vague, subjective, or opinionated annotations.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Object extraction used one worker per region description; freeform QA used eight QA pairs per image; region descriptions mention collecting 50 descriptions per image.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 33,000 unique crowd workers contributed; one example mentions a 'young Asian woman' only as image content, not worker demographics.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Stanford dependency parser was used to automatically extract nouns as suggestions for workers during object extraction.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset is biased toward images of people and certain sports, and answer distributions exhibit a long-tail pattern. The paper also notes annotation tendencies toward easy, frequently occurring relationships.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Freeform annotations create ambiguity in referring expressions and concept mappings; canonicalization to WordNet is imperfect and still ambiguous. The QA evaluation method also works poorly for long answers, and current captioning models fail to describe all events in an image.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Human-related attributes and categories such as gender/sex-coded references and age-related references are collected in annotations, along with activity/state descriptions of people.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for training and benchmarking cognitive scene understanding tasks, including object detection, segmentation, image captioning/region description generation, visual question answering, fine-grained recognition, activity recognition, reasoning, and scene graph-based modeling. The QA split uses 60% training and 40% test with image-exclusive partitions.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The paper mentions a first release of the dataset but does not provide an explicit maintenance, update schedule, maintainer, or deprecation policy.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Randomly sampled 500 attributes from each category to balance varying class sizes; used an 80/10/10 train/validation/test split over images.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Lowercased, lemmatized, and stripped excess whitespace from attributes; extracted noun phrases with Stanford NLP tools; mapped objects, attributes, relationships, and noun phrases to WordNet synsets; normalized attributes based on morphology (stemming); ignored prepositions for relationships; used parser-extracted nouns as suggestions during object extraction.
